materials.title: Learn: what living things need
materials.body: Living things need food, water and air to stay alive. Plants make their own food using sunlight; animals eat plants or other animals. A non-living thing, such as a rock, does not need food, water or air.

materials.title: Learn: living things grow and reproduce
materials.body: Living things grow: a kitten becomes a cat and a seed becomes a plant. Living things reproduce: they make young ones of their own kind. Non-living things do not grow or reproduce by themselves.

materials.title: Learn: living things respond to changes
materials.body: Living things respond to changes around them. A cat runs away from a loud noise. The leaves of a touch-me-not (mimosa) plant fold when touched. A plant on a window ledge bends towards the light.

materials.title: Learn: deciding if something is living
materials.body: To decide whether something is living, check the characteristics: it needs food, water and air; it grows; it reproduces; it responds to changes. Something must have all of these to be living. Fire can "grow" and needs air, but it does not reproduce like living things or need food and water, so it is non-living. A seed is living: it can grow into a new plant.

materials.title: Learn: flowering and non-flowering plants
materials.body: Plants can be grouped into flowering and non-flowering plants. Flowering plants (for example rose, hibiscus, rice, mango) produce flowers, and many form fruits with seeds. Non-flowering plants such as ferns and mosses do not produce flowers; they reproduce from spores.

materials.title: Learn: mammals
materials.body: Mammals have hair or fur on their bodies. Most mammals give birth to young ones alive, and all mammals feed their young with milk. Examples: dog, cat, human, whale, bat.

materials.title: Learn: birds and fish
materials.body: Birds have feathers, a beak and two wings, and lay eggs with hard shells. Not all birds can fly (a penguin cannot). Fish live in water, breathe with gills, have fins and most have scales.

materials.title: Learn: insects
materials.body: Insects have three body parts (head, thorax and abdomen) and six legs. Many have wings and feelers. Ants, butterflies, beetles and grasshoppers are insects. A spider has eight legs and two body parts, so it is not an insect.

materials.title: Learn: amphibians and reptiles
materials.body: Amphibians (frogs, toads) have moist, smooth skin and lay soft eggs in water; their young live in water. Reptiles (lizards, snakes, crocodiles, turtles) have dry, scaly skin and most lay eggs with leathery shells on land.

materials.title: Learn: fungi
materials.body: Fungi are living things that are neither plants nor animals. Examples are mushrooms, bread mould and yeast. Fungi cannot make their own food; they feed on dead or rotting things. Many reproduce from spores. They grow well in warm, damp places.

materials.title: Learn: bacteria
materials.body: Bacteria are tiny living things that can only be seen with a microscope. Some bacteria are useful, for example in making yoghurt. Some are harmful and can cause illness or make food go bad. Washing hands helps to remove harmful bacteria.

materials.title: Learn: common materials
materials.body: Objects are made of materials such as wood, metal, plastic, glass, ceramic, rubber and fabric. One object can be made of more than one material: a pencil has wood, graphite and sometimes a rubber eraser.

materials.title: Learn: strength and hardness
materials.body: Strength is how much load a material can hold before it breaks. Hardness is how difficult it is to scratch a material. A harder material can scratch a softer one. Metal is strong and hard; plastic is usually less hard than metal.

materials.title: Learn: flexibility
materials.body: A flexible material can bend without breaking. Rubber and fabric are flexible. Glass and ceramic are not flexible: they break if bent.

materials.title: Learn: waterproof and absorbent materials
materials.body: A waterproof material does not let water pass through (plastic, rubber, metal, glass). An absorbent material soaks up water (cotton, paper towel, sponge).

materials.title: Learn: allowing light through
materials.body: Some materials allow most light to pass through (clear glass, clear plastic). Some allow some light through (tracing paper, frosted glass). Some do not allow light through (wood, metal, cardboard).

materials.title: Learn: floating and sinking
materials.body: Some objects float on water and some sink. A cork, a wooden block and many plastic toys float. A metal key and a stone sink. Whether something floats depends on the material and the shape of the object.

materials.title: Learn: stages of a flowering plant
materials.body: A flowering plant grows from a seed. The seed germinates into a seedling, which grows into a young plant and then an adult plant. The adult plant produces flowers, the flowers become fruits, and the fruits contain seeds that can grow into new plants.

materials.title: Learn: what seeds need to germinate
materials.body: Seeds need water, air and warmth to germinate. They do not need light or soil to start germinating, because the seed has stored food. Green bean seeds on damp cotton wool in a warm place will germinate.

materials.title: Learn: inside a germinating seed
materials.body: A seed has a seed coat that protects it and seed leaves that store food. When a seed germinates, the young root comes out first and grows downwards; then the young shoot grows upwards.

materials.title: Learn: comparing plant life cycles
materials.body: Different flowering plants have the same stages, but the time taken can differ. A balsam plant may complete its life cycle in a few months; a mango tree takes years to produce fruits. Plants that reproduce from spores, like ferns, have a different life cycle.

materials.title: Learn: four-stage life cycles
materials.body: Some animals have four stages in their life cycle: egg → larva → pupa → adult. A butterfly is an example: the larva is a caterpillar and the pupa is a chrysalis. Mosquitoes and beetles also have four stages. The young looks very different from the adult.

materials.title: Learn: three-stage life cycles
materials.body: Some animals have three stages: egg → young → adult. A cockroach and a grasshopper have egg → nymph → adult; the nymph looks like a small adult without wings. A chicken has egg → chick → adult.

materials.title: Learn: the life cycle of a frog
materials.body: A frog has the life cycle egg → tadpole → young frog → adult frog. Tadpoles live in water and breathe with gills. As they grow, they grow legs and lose their tails; young frogs can then live on land.

materials.title: Learn: mosquitoes and stagnant water
materials.body: Mosquitoes lay eggs in stagnant (still) water. The larvae and pupae live in the water. Removing stagnant water from flowerpot plates, pails and drains stops mosquitoes from completing their life cycle and helps to prevent dengue.

materials.title: Learn: does the young look like the adult?
materials.body: In some life cycles the young looks like the adult (cockroach nymph, chick). In others the young looks very different (butterfly larva, mosquito larva, tadpole). Animals with a pupa stage have young that look very different from the adult.

materials.title: Learn: magnetic and non-magnetic materials
materials.body: Magnets attract magnetic materials such as iron and steel. Magnets do not attract non-magnetic materials such as copper, aluminium, plastic, wood, glass and paper. Not all metals are magnetic.

materials.title: Learn: the poles of a magnet
materials.body: Every magnet has two poles, a north pole (N) and a south pole (S). The magnetic force is strongest at the poles. If a bar magnet is dipped into paper clips, most clips stick near its two ends.

materials.title: Learn: like and unlike poles
materials.body: Unlike poles attract: N and S pull towards each other. Like poles repel: N and N, or S and S, push each other away.

materials.title: Learn: how to tell if something is a magnet
materials.body: A magnet attracts magnetic materials, so attraction alone does not prove that an object is a magnet: an iron bar is attracted too. Only repulsion proves it: if an object repels a magnet, the object must be a magnet.

materials.title: Learn: magnetic force through materials
materials.body: Magnetic force can act through non-magnetic materials such as paper, plastic, glass and water. A magnet under a table can move a paper clip on top of the table.

materials.title: Learn: a freely suspended magnet
materials.body: A bar magnet hung freely from a string comes to rest pointing in the north-south direction. Its north pole points north. A compass needle is a small magnet that works in this way.

materials.title: Learn: making a magnet by stroking
materials.body: A magnet can be made by stroking a steel or iron object with one pole of a magnet, in the same direction, many times. Lift the magnet away at the end of each stroke. More strokes usually make a stronger magnet. Only magnetic materials can be made into magnets.

materials.title: Learn: making an electromagnet
materials.body: A magnet can also be made using electricity: wind insulated wire around an iron nail and connect it to a battery. The nail becomes a magnet only while the current flows; this is an electromagnet. More turns of wire or more batteries make it stronger.

materials.title: Learn: temporary and permanent magnets
materials.body: Permanent magnets keep their magnetism for a long time. An electromagnet made with a soft iron core is a temporary magnet: it attracts steel when switched on and loses its magnetism when switched off. Dropping or heating a magnet can make it weaker.

materials.title: Learn: uses of magnets
materials.body: Magnets are used in daily life: fridge door seals, magnetic cupboard catches, compasses, pencil-case clasps, magnetic toys and sorting steel cans from aluminium cans for recycling.

items.stem: Which of these needs food, water and air to stay alive?
items.hint: Which one is living?
items.explanation: A goldfish is living, so it needs food, water and air.

items.stem: A plant is kept in a sealed box with no air for many days. What will most likely happen?

options.text: It will turn into a rock.

items.hint: Think about what all living things need.
items.explanation: Plants need air to stay alive, so it will die.

items.stem: Which is NOT a need of living things?
items.hint: Living things need three main things to survive.
items.explanation: Living things need food, water and air. Sand is not a need.

items.stem: A hamster is given food and air but no water for a long time. What will happen to it?
items.hint: Water is one of the needs of all living things.
items.explanation: Without water the hamster cannot stay alive.

items.stem: Mei forgot to water her potted plant for two weeks. The leaves dried up. What does this show?

options.text: Plants need sand to stay alive.
Plants need water to stay alive.

items.hint: What was missing?
items.explanation: The plant lacked water, showing plants need water to survive.

items.stem: Which shows that a kitten is a living thing?
items.hint: Which change happens only to living things?
items.explanation: Growing is a characteristic of living things.

items.stem: A hen lays eggs that hatch into chicks. Which characteristic of living things does this show?

options.text: Living things are made of metal.

items.hint: The hen makes young of its own kind.
items.explanation: Making young ones is reproduction.

items.stem: Which characteristic do all living things have?
items.hint: Think of something true for both plants and animals.
items.explanation: All living things reproduce. Not all can fly or have legs, and only plants make food.

items.stem: A balloon gets bigger when air is blown into it. Is the balloon a living thing?

options.text: No, it gets bigger only because air is put in.

items.hint: Does the balloon grow by itself?
items.explanation: The balloon does not grow by itself or reproduce, so it is non-living.

items.stem: A small mango tree grows taller and later produces fruits with seeds. Which two characteristics does this show?

options.text: It moves and it breathes fire.
It is hard and it is green.

items.hint: Taller, then seeds for new plants.
items.explanation: Growing taller is growth; seeds make new plants, which is reproduction.

items.stem: The leaves of a mimosa plant fold up when Ali touches them. What does this show?
items.hint: The plant reacted to being touched.
items.explanation: Folding when touched is a response to change.

items.stem: Which is an example of a living thing responding to a change?

options.text: A ball bounces on the floor.
A dog barks when a stranger comes near.
A stone rolls down a slope.

items.hint: Which one involves a living thing?
items.explanation: The dog reacts to a stranger: a response by a living thing.

items.stem: A plant on a window ledge bends towards the window. What is it responding to?
items.hint: What comes in through a window?
items.explanation: The plant responds to light by growing towards it.

items.stem: A snail pulls its body into its shell when touched. What does this show?
items.hint: What happened just before it pulled in?
items.explanation: Pulling in when touched is a response to a change.

items.stem: When it gets dark, the leaves of some plants close up. Which characteristic of living things is shown?
items.hint: Something around the plant changed.
items.explanation: The change from light to dark caused a response.

items.stem: Which of these is a living thing?
items.hint: Which can grow into a new plant?
items.explanation: A seed is living because it can grow into a new plant.

items.stem: Ben says fire is living because it gets bigger and needs air. Why is he wrong?

options.text: Fire does not reproduce or need food and water like living things.

items.hint: Check all the characteristics, not just two.
items.explanation: A living thing must have all the characteristics. Fire does not.

items.stem: Which group contains only living things?
items.hint: Check each item in the group.
items.explanation: A mushroom (fungus), a fern (plant) and an ant (animal) are all living.

items.stem: Which group contains only non-living things?
items.hint: Remove any group that has a living thing.
items.explanation: Water, sand and a battery are all non-living.

items.stem: A robot dog can walk and bark. Is it a living thing?

options.text: No, it cannot grow or reproduce.

items.hint: Moving and making sounds is not enough.
items.explanation: The robot does not grow or reproduce, so it is non-living.

items.stem: Which plant is a non-flowering plant?
items.hint: Which one reproduces from spores?
items.explanation: A fern does not produce flowers; it reproduces from spores.

items.stem: Moss grows on a damp wall but never produces flowers. How does it reproduce?
items.hint: It has no flowers, so it has no seeds from fruits.
items.explanation: Mosses are non-flowering plants that reproduce from spores.

items.stem: Which plant produces flowers?
items.hint: Its name gives a clue.
items.explanation: A sunflower is a flowering plant. A mushroom is not a plant at all.

items.stem: Small brown dots are found under the leaves of a plant that never flowers. What are they likely to be?
items.hint: Non-flowering plants such as ferns have these under their leaves.
items.explanation: Ferns carry spores in small cases under their leaves.

items.stem: A plant has fruits with seeds inside. Which group does it belong to?
items.hint: Fruits come from flowers.
items.explanation: Fruits develop from flowers, so it is a flowering plant.

items.stem: Which animal is a mammal?
items.hint: Which one feeds its young with milk?
items.explanation: A whale feeds its young with milk and is a mammal, even though it lives in the sea.

items.stem: Which feature tells us that a bat is a mammal?

options.text: It has fur and feeds its young with milk.

items.hint: Birds can fly too. Look for a mammal feature.
items.explanation: Fur and feeding young with milk are mammal features.

items.stem: Which is a feature of all mammals?

options.text: They feed their young with milk.

items.hint: Think of how a mother dog feeds her puppies.
items.explanation: All mammals feed their young with milk.

items.stem: A dolphin lives in the sea and has smooth skin. It breathes air and feeds its young with milk. Which group does it belong to?
items.hint: Feeding young with milk is the key feature.
items.explanation: Dolphins feed their young with milk, so they are mammals.

items.stem: Ali's pet has fur and gives birth to young ones alive. Which group does it belong to?
items.hint: Fur is a clue.
items.explanation: Fur and giving birth to young alive are mammal features.

items.stem: Which feature do ALL birds have?
items.hint: A penguin is a bird but cannot fly.
items.explanation: All birds have feathers; not all birds can fly.

items.stem: An animal lives in water, has fins and breathes through gills. Which group is it in?
items.hint: Which group uses gills?
items.explanation: Fins and gills are features of fish.

items.stem: Which animal is a bird?
items.hint: Look for feathers and a beak.
items.explanation: An ostrich has feathers and a beak, so it is a bird, even though it cannot fly.

items.stem: How do fish take in air from the water?
items.hint: Look at the openings at the side of a fish's head.
items.explanation: Fish breathe using gills.

items.stem: A penguin swims well and cannot fly. Why is it still a bird?

options.text: It has feathers and a beak and lays eggs.

items.hint: Use bird features, not where it lives.
items.explanation: Feathers, a beak and laying eggs make a penguin a bird.

items.stem: How many legs does an insect have?
items.hint: Count the legs of an ant.
items.explanation: All insects have six legs.

items.stem: Why is a spider not an insect?
items.hint: Count its legs.
items.explanation: Insects have six legs; a spider has eight.

items.stem: Which animal is an insect?
items.hint: Look for six legs and three body parts.
items.explanation: A grasshopper has six legs and three body parts.

items.stem: An animal has 3 body parts, 6 legs and 2 feelers. Which group does it belong to?
items.hint: Six legs is the key.
items.explanation: Three body parts and six legs show it is an insect.

items.stem: Mei found a small creature with 8 legs in the garden. Is it an insect?

options.text: Yes, all small creatures are insects.
No, because it is in the garden.

items.hint: Count the legs.
items.explanation: With 8 legs, it is not an insect.

items.stem: Which animal is a reptile?
items.hint: Look for dry, scaly skin.
items.explanation: A lizard has dry, scaly skin, so it is a reptile.

items.stem: A frog has moist skin and lays eggs in water. Which group does it belong to?
items.hint: Moist skin and eggs in water are clues.
items.explanation: Frogs are amphibians.

items.stem: What kind of skin do reptiles have?
items.hint: Think of a crocodile.
items.explanation: Reptiles have dry, scaly skin.

items.stem: Where do frogs usually lay their eggs?

options.text: in a nest on a tree

items.hint: Think about where tadpoles swim.
items.explanation: Frogs lay their eggs in water.

items.stem: A turtle has a hard shell and dry, scaly skin, and lays eggs in sand. Which group does it belong to?
items.hint: Dry, scaly skin is a clue.
items.explanation: Dry, scaly skin and eggs laid on land show it is a reptile.

items.stem: Which is a fungus?
items.hint: Which one cannot make its own food?
items.explanation: A mushroom is a fungus. Ferns, moss and grass are plants.

items.stem: Black fuzzy spots grew on a slice of bread left in a damp cupboard. What are they?
items.hint: It grew on food in a warm, damp place.
items.explanation: Bread mould is a fungus.

items.stem: How do fungi get their food?

options.text: They feed on dead or rotting things.

items.hint: Fungi are not green plants.
items.explanation: Fungi cannot make food; they feed on dead or rotting matter.

items.stem: Where is bread mould most likely to grow quickly?
items.hint: Fungi like warmth and moisture.
items.explanation: Fungi grow well in warm, damp places.

items.stem: Why are mushrooms not grouped as plants?

options.text: They cannot make their own food.

items.hint: What can plants do that fungi cannot?
items.explanation: Plants make their own food; fungi cannot.

items.stem: How can we see bacteria?
items.hint: Bacteria are very tiny.
items.explanation: Bacteria are too small to see without a microscope.

items.stem: Which shows that some bacteria are useful?

options.text: They are used to make yoghurt.

items.hint: Look for a helpful use.
items.explanation: Some bacteria help to turn milk into yoghurt.

items.stem: Why should we wash our hands before eating?
items.hint: Some tiny living things on hands can make us ill.
items.explanation: Washing removes harmful bacteria.

items.stem: Milk left out on a hot day turned sour. What most likely caused this?
items.hint: Tiny living things grow in food.
items.explanation: Bacteria growing in the milk made it go sour.

items.stem: Which statement about bacteria is correct?

options.text: Some are useful and some are harmful.

items.hint: Think of yoghurt and of illness.
items.explanation: Bacteria can be both useful and harmful.

items.stem: A spoon is hard, shiny and cold to touch. Which material is it most likely made of?
items.hint: Think of cutlery at home.
items.explanation: Shiny, hard spoons are usually made of metal.

items.stem: Which object is usually made of glass?
items.hint: Which one lets you see through it?
items.explanation: Window panes are usually made of glass.

items.stem: What material is a rubber band made of?
items.hint: Its name is a clue.
items.explanation: Rubber bands are made of rubber.

items.stem: A cup is hard, breaks easily when dropped and is not see-through. Which material is it most likely made of?
items.hint: Think of a mug from the kitchen.
items.explanation: Ceramic cups are hard, break easily and do not let light through.

items.stem: A chair has a seat of fabric, legs of metal and armrests of wood. How many different materials is it made of?
items.hint: Count the different materials named.
items.explanation: Fabric, metal and wood: 3 materials.

items.stem: Which material is used for bridges because it is strong?
items.hint: A bridge must hold heavy loads.
items.explanation: Steel is strong and can hold heavy loads.

items.stem: Ali scratched block A with block B and a mark appeared on block A. What can he conclude?

options.text: A and B are equally hard.

items.hint: The harder material scratches the softer one.
items.explanation: Since B scratched A, B is harder.

items.stem: Which property tells us how difficult it is to scratch a material?
items.hint: Think of scratching with a nail.
items.explanation: Hardness is how difficult a material is to scratch.

items.stem: Strips of different materials of the same size are loaded with weights until they break. What property is being tested?
items.hint: Loads are added until the material breaks.
items.explanation: Strength is how much load a material can hold before breaking.

items.stem: Why is a cutting board in a kitchen often made of hard wood or plastic and not of soft sponge?

options.text: It needs to be hard so knives do not cut through easily.

items.hint: What happens when a knife presses on it?
items.explanation: A hard material resists cuts from knives.

items.stem: Which material is the most flexible?
items.hint: Which can bend and not break?
items.explanation: Rubber can bend easily without breaking.

items.stem: A garden hose bends around corners without breaking. Which property does it show?
items.hint: It bends easily.
items.explanation: Bending without breaking is flexibility.

items.stem: Why are swimming caps made of rubber?
items.hint: The cap must stretch over the head and keep water out.
items.explanation: Flexible, waterproof rubber fits snugly and keeps water out.

items.stem: Which object would break if you tried to bend it?
items.hint: Which material is not flexible?
items.explanation: Glass is not flexible and breaks when bent.

items.stem: Four strips of different materials have the same length, width and thickness. Each is fixed at one end, with the same small weight hung from the other end. None breaks. W bends down 1 cm, X 3 cm, Y 4 cm and Z 5 cm. Which conclusion is supported?
items.hint: Compare how far the strips bend under the same load.
items.explanation: W bends the least under the same load. Of these equal-sized strips, W is the least flexible.

items.stem: Which material is best for a raincoat?
items.hint: A raincoat must stop water getting through.
items.explanation: Plastic is waterproof.

items.stem: Which material should a towel be made of?
items.hint: A towel must soak up water.
items.explanation: Cotton is absorbent.

items.stem: Which material is absorbent?
items.hint: Which one soaks up water?
items.explanation: Paper towels absorb water.

items.stem: Mei spilled water on a table. Which material is best for wiping it up?
items.hint: Choose the one that soaks up water.
items.explanation: A sponge absorbs water well.

items.stem: Why is an umbrella made of plastic-coated fabric and not plain paper?

options.text: Plastic-coated fabric is waterproof and does not tear easily when wet.

items.hint: What happens to paper in rain?
items.explanation: Paper absorbs water and tears; the coated fabric is waterproof.

items.stem: Which material allows most light to pass through?
items.hint: You can see clearly through it.
items.explanation: Clear glass lets most light pass through.

items.stem: Why is a bathroom window often made of frosted glass?

options.text: It lets some light in but people cannot see in clearly.

items.hint: Light is needed, but privacy too.
items.explanation: Frosted glass lets some light through and gives privacy.

items.stem: Which material does NOT allow light to pass through?
items.hint: Which one is not see-through at all?
items.explanation: Wood blocks light.

items.stem: A torch shines on a sheet. The light on the wall behind is dim but not dark. What does this show?

options.text: The sheet allows some light through.
The sheet allows all light through.
The sheet allows no light through.

items.hint: Some light reached the wall.
items.explanation: Dim light means some, but not all, light passed through.

items.stem: Which material is best for the window of a toy oven so you can see the cake?
items.hint: You need to see inside.
items.explanation: Clear glass lets light through so the cake can be seen.

items.stem: Which object is most likely to float on water?
items.hint: Think of corks bobbing on water.
items.explanation: A cork floats.

items.stem: Ali drops a steel nail and a wooden stick into a tank of water. What happens?

options.text: The nail floats and the stick sinks.
The nail sinks and the stick floats.

items.hint: Think about metal and wood in water.
items.explanation: Steel nails sink; wood floats.

items.stem: Which material is used for life jackets because it floats?
items.hint: A life jacket must keep you up.
items.explanation: Foam floats and keeps a swimmer up.

items.stem: A toy boat is made to float. Which material would be the worst choice for it?
items.hint: Which one sinks?
items.explanation: Stone sinks, so it is the worst choice.

items.stem: A plastic bottle with its cap on floats. Water is poured in until it is full and the cap is put back on. It now sinks. What changed?

options.text: It was filled with water instead of air.

items.hint: Compare what was inside the bottle.
items.explanation: Replacing the air inside with water made it sink.

items.stem: What is the correct order of the life cycle of a flowering plant?

options.text: seed → adult plant → seedling → young plant
seed → seedling → young plant → adult plant
seedling → seed → adult plant → young plant
adult plant → seed → young plant → seedling

items.hint: Start with the stage that is planted in soil.
items.explanation: A seed germinates into a seedling, then a young plant, then an adult plant.

items.stem: Where are new seeds formed in a flowering plant?
items.hint: What do you find when you cut open a papaya?
items.explanation: Seeds are formed inside fruits.

items.stem: Which stage comes right after a seed germinates?
items.hint: It is a very young plant with its first leaves.
items.explanation: After germination, the seed becomes a seedling.

items.stem: A flower falls off a tomato plant and a small green tomato appears. What is this stage?
items.hint: Fruits come from flowers.
items.explanation: The flower develops into a fruit.

items.stem: A papaya fruit is cut open and many black seeds are found. Why are seeds important to the plant?

options.text: They can grow into new plants.

items.hint: Think about how plants reproduce.
items.explanation: Seeds grow into new plants, continuing the life cycle.

items.stem: Which set of conditions is needed for seeds to germinate?
items.hint: Seeds can germinate on damp cotton wool.
items.explanation: Seeds need water, air and warmth to germinate.

items.stem: Green bean seeds are placed on dry cotton wool in a warm room. They do not germinate. What is missing?
items.hint: Look at the word "dry".
items.explanation: Without water, seeds cannot germinate.

items.stem: Seeds on damp cotton wool in a dark cupboard germinate. What does this show?

options.text: Light is not needed for germination.

items.hint: Was there light in the cupboard?
items.explanation: They germinated in the dark, so light is not needed.

items.stem: Why can a seed germinate even without soil?

options.text: It has stored food inside it.

items.hint: Where does a young seedling get food before its leaves open?
items.explanation: The seed leaves store food for the young plant.

items.stem: Ali places seeds in two dishes with damp cotton wool. Dish A is in a fridge; Dish B is in a warm room. Only Dish B germinates. What does this show?
items.hint: What is different between the two dishes?
items.explanation: Only temperature differed, so warmth is needed.

items.stem: What comes out of a germinating seed first?
items.hint: It anchors the seedling and takes in water.
items.explanation: The young root appears first.

items.stem: What is the job of the seed coat?

options.text: to take in water from soil

items.hint: It is the outer covering.
items.explanation: The seed coat protects the parts inside.

items.stem: What do the seed leaves of a green bean seedling provide?

options.text: stored food for the young plant

items.hint: Before its true leaves can make food, the seedling uses this.
items.explanation: Seed leaves store food for the young plant.

items.stem: In which direction does the young root grow?
items.hint: Roots grow into the soil.
items.explanation: The young root grows downwards.

items.stem: The seed leaves of a seedling shrink as it grows. Why?

options.text: They are eaten by the soil.
The stored food is used up by the growing plant.

items.hint: What is stored in seed leaves?
items.explanation: The young plant uses up the food stored in them.

items.stem: Which stage do a balsam plant and a mango tree both have?
items.hint: Both are flowering plants.
items.explanation: Both are flowering plants, so both produce flowers and fruits.

items.stem: Why might a farmer grow balsam rather than mango to show children a whole life cycle in one school term?

options.text: Balsam completes its life cycle much faster.

items.hint: Compare how long each takes.
items.explanation: Balsam completes its life cycle in months; mango takes years.

items.stem: Which plant does NOT grow from a seed?
items.hint: Which one reproduces from spores?
items.explanation: Ferns reproduce from spores, not seeds.

items.stem: Which statement about flowering plants is correct?

options.text: They have the same stages but may take different lengths of time.
They all take one week to grow.

items.hint: Compare balsam and mango.
items.explanation: Same stages, different durations.

items.stem: A chilli plant produced its first fruits 3 months after the seed was planted. Which stage came just before the fruits?
items.hint: Fruits develop from something.
items.explanation: Fruits develop from flowers.

items.stem: What is the correct order of a butterfly's life cycle?
items.hint: The caterpillar comes before the chrysalis.
items.explanation: Egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa (chrysalis), adult.

items.stem: At which stage does a butterfly eat a lot of leaves?
items.hint: Caterpillars are hungry eaters.
items.explanation: The larva (caterpillar) feeds on leaves.

items.stem: What is the pupa stage of a butterfly also called?
items.hint: It is the hard case where the change happens.
items.explanation: A butterfly's pupa is called a chrysalis.

items.stem: Which animal has a four-stage life cycle?
items.hint: Look for a larva and a pupa stage.
items.explanation: Mosquitoes go through egg, larva, pupa and adult.

items.stem: A beetle's young looks like a worm and does not look like the adult. Which stage is this?
items.hint: In a four-stage life cycle, the worm-like young is the...
items.explanation: The worm-like young of a beetle is the larva.

items.stem: What is the young of a cockroach called?
items.hint: It looks like a small adult without wings.
items.explanation: A young cockroach is a nymph.

items.stem: Which animal has a three-stage life cycle?
items.hint: It has no pupa stage.
items.explanation: A grasshopper goes through egg, nymph and adult.

items.stem: How is a cockroach nymph different from an adult cockroach?

options.text: It has no wings and is smaller.

items.hint: The nymph looks like a small adult.
items.explanation: A nymph is smaller and has no wings.

items.stem: Which life cycle has only three stages?
items.hint: Which one has no larva or pupa?
items.explanation: A chicken goes egg → chick → adult.

items.stem: An insect's young looks like a small adult but has no wings. How many stages does its life cycle most likely have?
items.hint: There is no pupa stage when the young already looks like the adult.
items.explanation: Egg, nymph, adult: three stages.

items.stem: What hatches from a frog's egg?
items.hint: It lives in water and has a tail.
items.explanation: A tadpole hatches from a frog's egg.

items.stem: What happens to a tadpole's tail as it grows into a frog?
items.hint: Adult frogs do not have tails.
items.explanation: The tail shortens and disappears.

items.stem: What is the correct order of a frog's life cycle?

options.text: egg → young frog → tadpole → adult frog
tadpole → egg → adult frog → young frog
egg → tadpole → young frog → adult frog

items.hint: The tadpole comes before the frog with legs.
items.explanation: Egg, tadpole, young frog, adult frog.

items.stem: Where do tadpoles live?
items.hint: They have tails for swimming.
items.explanation: Tadpoles live in water.

items.stem: A young frog has four legs and a short tail. Which stage came just before it?
items.hint: What does a frog look like before it has legs?
items.explanation: Before growing legs, it was a tadpole.

items.stem: Where do mosquitoes lay their eggs?
items.hint: Their larvae live in water.
items.explanation: Mosquitoes lay eggs in stagnant water.

items.stem: Why should we turn over pails after use?

options.text: so that the pail dries faster for painting
so that water does not collect for mosquitoes to breed

items.hint: Think about where mosquitoes lay eggs.
items.explanation: Removing stagnant water stops mosquitoes breeding.

items.stem: In which stages does a mosquito live in water?
items.hint: The adult flies; the young stages need water.
items.explanation: Mosquito larvae and pupae live in water.

items.stem: Which action helps to prevent dengue?
items.hint: Stop mosquitoes from breeding.
items.explanation: Removing stagnant water prevents mosquito breeding.

items.stem: Wriggling creatures are seen in a pail of rainwater left outside for a week. What are they most likely to be?
items.hint: Which insect breeds in still water?
items.explanation: Mosquito larvae wriggle in stagnant water.

items.stem: Which young animal looks most like its adult?
items.hint: Which young has the same body shape as the adult?
items.explanation: A cockroach nymph looks like a small adult without wings.

items.stem: Which young animal looks very different from its adult?
items.hint: Think of the animal that later forms a chrysalis.
items.explanation: A caterpillar looks very different from a butterfly.

items.stem: Animals with a pupa stage have young that ___.

options.text: look very different from the adult

items.hint: Think of the butterfly.
items.explanation: Young with a pupa stage look very different from the adult.

items.stem: Which pair has young that look different from their adults?
items.hint: Caterpillars and tadpoles.
items.explanation: Caterpillars and tadpoles look very different from their adults.

items.stem: A young animal lives in water and the adult lives on land and hops. Which animal is it?
items.hint: Which young lives in water?
items.explanation: A tadpole lives in water and grows into a hopping frog.

items.stem: Which object will be attracted to a magnet?
items.hint: Which metal is magnetic?
items.explanation: Iron is a magnetic material.

items.stem: Ali says all metals are attracted to magnets. Which object shows he is wrong?
items.hint: Find a metal that is not magnetic.
items.explanation: Aluminium is a metal but is not magnetic.

items.stem: Which material is magnetic?
items.hint: Some metals are magnetic, but not all metals are.
items.explanation: Steel is magnetic.

items.stem: A magnet is moved over a pile of objects. Which object stays behind?
items.hint: Which material is non-magnetic?
items.explanation: Copper is non-magnetic, so it stays behind.

items.stem: Mei wants to pick up spilled pins quickly. Why does using a magnet work?

options.text: The pins are made of copper.
The pins are made of plastic.
The pins are made of steel, a magnetic material.

items.hint: What are pins usually made of?
items.explanation: Steel pins are attracted to the magnet.

items.stem: Where is the magnetic force of a bar magnet strongest?
items.hint: Where do most paper clips stick?
items.explanation: The force is strongest at the poles.

items.stem: A bar magnet is dipped into iron filings. Where will most filings collect?
items.hint: Think about the poles.
items.explanation: Most filings collect at the poles, at both ends.

items.stem: How many poles does a bar magnet have?
items.hint: One is north, one is south.
items.explanation: A magnet has a north pole and a south pole.

items.stem: A ring magnet attracts most pins at its two flat faces. What does this show?

options.text: The poles are at the flat faces.
The poles are at its edge only.

items.hint: The force is strongest at the poles.
items.explanation: Most pins stick where the poles are, at the flat faces.

items.stem: A bar magnet is broken in half. How many poles does each piece have?
items.hint: Every magnet has two poles.
items.explanation: Each piece becomes a magnet with its own N and S poles.

items.stem: What happens when the N pole of one magnet is brought near the S pole of another?
items.hint: Unlike poles...
items.explanation: Unlike poles attract.

items.stem: Two magnets push each other away. Which poles are facing each other?
items.hint: Like poles repel.
items.explanation: Like poles, such as S and S, repel.

items.stem: Which pair of poles repel?
items.hint: Like poles...
items.explanation: Like poles repel: N and N.

items.stem: Two ring magnets on a pencil float one above the other without touching. Why?

options.text: Unlike poles face each other and attract.
Like poles face each other and repel.

items.hint: Something is pushing the top magnet up.
items.explanation: Facing like poles repel, holding the top magnet up.

items.stem: Magnet P's north pole attracts end X of magnet Q. What is end X?
items.hint: Unlike poles attract.
items.explanation: A north pole attracts a south pole, so X is S.

items.stem: Which observation proves that bar X is a magnet?

options.text: X is attracted to a magnet.
One end of X repels the N pole of a magnet.

items.hint: Can an iron bar repel a magnet?
items.explanation: Only a magnet can repel a magnet.

items.stem: Bar Y is attracted to both poles of a magnet. What can you conclude?

options.text: Y is a magnetic material but not necessarily a magnet.

items.hint: A magnet would repel one of the poles.
items.explanation: Being attracted to both poles means Y is magnetic, not a magnet.

items.stem: Why can attraction alone not prove that an object is a magnet?

options.text: Magnetic materials are also attracted to magnets.

items.hint: Think of an iron nail.
items.explanation: Iron is attracted to magnets but is not a magnet.

items.stem: Ali tests three rods. Rod A repels a magnet. Rod B is attracted to both poles. Rod C is not attracted. Which rod is a magnet?
items.hint: Look for repulsion.
items.explanation: Only rod A shows repulsion.

items.stem: A steel bar is attracted to the N pole of a magnet. What test should be done next to find out if it is a magnet?

options.text: Bring the other end of the bar near the same N pole and check for repulsion.

items.hint: A magnet shows repulsion with like poles.
items.explanation: Checking for repulsion confirms whether it is a magnet.

items.stem: A magnet under a thin wooden table moves a paper clip on top. What does this show?

options.text: Magnetic force can pass through wood.

items.hint: The table is between them.
items.explanation: The magnetic force acted through the non-magnetic wood.

items.stem: A paper clip in a glass of water is pulled up the side by a magnet outside the glass. What does this show?

options.text: Magnetic force can pass through glass and water.

items.hint: What is between the magnet and the clip?
items.explanation: The force acted through glass and water.

items.stem: Through which material can magnetic force act?
items.hint: Think of fridge magnets holding notes.
items.explanation: Fridge magnets hold paper because the force acts through paper.

items.stem: A magnet holds a sheet of paper on a steel fridge door. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The magnetic force passes through the paper to the steel door.
The paper is attracted to the magnet.

items.hint: Is paper magnetic?
items.explanation: The force passes through the paper to the steel door.

items.stem: Mei adds sheets of paper between a magnet and a paper clip one at a time. The clip falls after 20 sheets. What does this show?

options.text: Magnets get stronger with more paper.
The magnetic force gets weaker with greater distance.

items.hint: More sheets means the magnet is further away.
items.explanation: The force weakens as the distance increases.

items.stem: A bar magnet hangs freely from a string. Which direction does it come to rest in?
items.hint: This is how a compass works.
items.explanation: A freely suspended magnet points north-south.

items.stem: Why does a compass needle point north?

options.text: It is heavy at one end.

items.hint: What kind of object behaves like a hanging bar magnet?
items.explanation: A compass needle is a magnet, so it points north-south.

items.stem: Which end of a freely hanging magnet points north?
items.hint: The poles are named after this.
items.explanation: The north pole points north.

items.stem: An iron bar hangs freely and stops in different directions each time. What does this show?

options.text: The iron bar is a magnet.
The iron bar is not a magnet.

items.hint: A magnet would always stop north-south.
items.explanation: Not settling north-south shows it is not a magnet.

items.stem: Hikers use a compass to find their way. Which property of magnets do they use?

options.text: A freely moving magnet points north-south.

items.hint: The needle is a magnet.
items.explanation: The compass needle points north-south, showing direction.

items.stem: Which object can be made into a magnet by stroking?
items.hint: Only magnetic materials can become magnets.
items.explanation: Steel is magnetic, so it can be magnetised.

items.stem: How should a steel bar be stroked to make it a magnet?

options.text: with both poles, back and forth
with one pole, in one direction, many times

items.hint: The strokes must all go the same way.
items.explanation: Stroke with one pole in one direction many times.

items.stem: Why can a copper rod not be made into a magnet?
items.hint: Which materials can become magnets?
items.explanation: Only magnetic materials can be magnetised.

items.stem: Ali stroked steel nail A 10 times and steel nail B 40 times in the same way. Which is likely to pick up more pins?
items.hint: More strokes...
items.explanation: More strokes usually make a stronger magnet.

items.stem: Mei stroked a steel pin back and forth with a magnet. It did not become a magnet. What did she do wrong?

options.text: She did not stroke in one direction only.

items.hint: The direction of stroking matters.
items.explanation: Strokes must be in one direction only.

items.stem: What is needed to make an electromagnet?

options.text: an iron nail, wire coiled round it and a battery

items.hint: Electricity must flow around a magnetic material.
items.explanation: A coil of wire around an iron nail connected to a battery makes an electromagnet.

items.stem: What happens when the battery of an electromagnet is disconnected?

options.text: It loses most of its magnetism.

items.hint: It works only while current flows.
items.explanation: An electromagnet works only while current flows.

items.stem: How can an electromagnet be made stronger?

options.text: by adding more turns of wire

items.hint: Think about the coil.
items.explanation: More turns of wire make it stronger.

items.stem: Why is an iron nail used inside the coil instead of a wooden stick?
items.hint: Which material can become a magnet?
items.explanation: Iron can be magnetised; wood cannot.

items.stem: A crane in a scrapyard lifts cars with a large electromagnet and drops them when it switches off. Why is an electromagnet used and not a permanent magnet?

options.text: It can be switched off to release the cars.

items.hint: Think about letting go of the load.
items.explanation: Switching off the current releases the load.

items.stem: Which is a temporary magnet?

options.text: a bar magnet in a box

items.hint: Which one stops working when switched off?
items.explanation: An electromagnet is a temporary magnet.

items.stem: A scrapyard crane has an electromagnet. It picks up steel cans when switched on and releases them when switched off. Which description fits this magnet?

options.text: It stays magnetic after it is switched off.

items.hint: Think about what changes when the power is switched off.
items.explanation: The electromagnet loses its magnetism when switched off, so it is a temporary magnet.

items.stem: Which action can weaken a magnet?

options.text: using it to pick up pins

items.hint: Rough handling affects magnets.
items.explanation: Dropping a magnet can weaken it.

items.stem: Which is a permanent magnet?

options.text: an iron nail with no magnetism

items.hint: Which keeps its magnetism for a long time?
items.explanation: Fridge magnets are permanent magnets.

items.stem: A magnet that was left near a hot stove became weaker. What caused this?
items.hint: Think about what weakens magnets.
items.explanation: Heating can weaken a magnet.

items.stem: Why does a fridge door close tightly?

options.text: The door is made of glass.
There are magnets in the door seal.

items.hint: The seal sticks to the steel body.
items.explanation: Magnetic strips in the seal hold the door closed.

items.stem: At a recycling centre, how can steel cans be separated from aluminium cans?
items.hint: Which metal is magnetic?
items.explanation: Steel cans are attracted to a magnet; aluminium cans are not.

items.stem: Which item uses a magnet?
items.hint: It shows direction.
items.explanation: A compass needle is a magnet.

items.stem: A cupboard door stays shut because a magnet holds a small steel plate. Which property of magnets is used?
items.hint: The plate is steel.
items.explanation: The magnet attracts the steel plate.

items.stem: A toy train's carriages join with magnets at each end. Sometimes two carriages push apart. Why?

options.text: Like poles are facing each other.
The carriages are made of copper.
Unlike poles are facing each other.

items.hint: Like poles...
items.explanation: Facing like poles repel, so the carriages push apart.
